title: The Most Important Memory is Still the One Inside Your Head
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick uses a new paper by Barbara Oakley, Terrence Sejnowski and colleagues to argue that education's decades-long retreat from memorisation, now accelerated by smartphones and AI, rests on a misunderstanding of how the brain learns. He traces the anti-memorisation orthodoxy through Reform Mathematics, Whole Language, Bloom's Taxonomy, 21st Century Skills frameworks and PISA. Drawing on the study, he explains how expertise emerges when knowledge moves from the declarative to the procedural memory system, using the drummer as an image of automaticity freeing bandwidth for creativity. He then shows how internally stored knowledge powers prediction error, the brain's mechanism for spotting mistakes, with a Year 6 multiplication example, and cites studies in which students using ChatGPT or GPT-4 performed well in the moment but learned little, which he calls 'cognitive karaoke'. He closes with classroom implications, including practising to automaticity and using AI as an amplifier rather than a replacement, and a lament for what cognitive offloading may cost.
points: Hendrick argues that the belief that memorisation is unnecessary in an age of easy information access became an uncontested educational orthodoxy through movements like Reform Mathematics, Whole Language and Bloom's Taxonomy.
Drawing on Oakley and Sejnowski, he explains that expertise emerges when knowledge transitions from declarative to procedural memory, and that constant outsourcing prevents that transition.
His prediction-error example shows a student who has memorised times tables instantly flags 8 x 7 = 102, while a calculator-dependent classmate has no internal expectation to violate.
He cites studies where AI-assisted students outperformed peers during practice but collapsed on unaided exams, calling this 'cognitive karaoke', a performance of mastery without memory.
His practical implications include practising basics to automaticity, aiming for roughly 85% accuracy, and using AI as an amplifier only once solid internal knowledge exists.
quotes: Over the last 50 years, the idea that memorisation is much less important than generalised critical thinking became a largely uncontested orthodoxy in education. Of course, rote memorisation of disconnected facts without linking them to broader concepts and ideas is a joyless, pointless enterprise but recent research suggests we may have thrown the baby out with the bathwater, creating a false dichotomy between memory and understanding that has undermined the very cognitive foundations we sought to strengthen.

The problem isn't memorisation itself, but a misunderstanding of how memory actually works. When we memorise multiplication tables or vocabulary words, we're not just storing isolated facts, we're building structured knowledge that enables mathematical intuition and sophisticated reasoning.

This is expertise: not conscious calculation, but fluency born of deep practice. The paradox is that by memorising so much you can actually forget about the very thing that took up all your cognitive bandwidth.

Now consider her classmate who never memorised multiplication tables and relies exclusively on a calculator. Presented with the same incorrect answer, there is no internal expectation to violate, no alarm bell to ring. The error may pass unnoticed, unchallenged, a kind of cognitive passivity that leaves her at the mercy of external tools.

Recent studies reveal how AI tools can amplify these problems. College students using ChatGPT to write essays produced higher-quality work but showed no actual knowledge improvement when tested later. In other words, they were performing knowing without actually knowing.

Build Procedural Fluency: Certain basics like multiplication tables, vocabulary, scientific formulas etc should be practiced to automaticity. This isn't mindless drilling; it's creating the cognitive infrastructure that enables later complex thinking and creativity.
The very architecture of expertise is built not by exposure, but by effort. Without internalised knowledge, there is no deep understanding, no flexible thinking, no meaningful creativity.
